title: Area VII review: Emergency Operations
intro: These questions mix the two single-engine Tasks of Area VII, loss of communications and an approach with failed primary flight instruments. Many of them join both Tasks in one IFR flight where things start to go wrong, just like the checkride.

questions.q: You took off at 1400Z with a filed ETE of 2:00. En route you told Center about a strong headwind and amended your ETE to 2:20. Later the radios fail in IMC. Your clearance limit is the destination IAF and you have no EFC. You reach the IAF at 1608Z. When should you begin descent and the approach?
options: On arrival at the IAF, at 1608Z
As close as possible to 1600Z, the ETA from your filed ETE
As close as possible to 1620Z, the ETA from your amended ETE
As close as possible to 1630Z, adding a 10 minute margin for ATC
questions.why: With no EFC, begin as close as possible to the ETA calculated from the filed or amended (with ATC) ETE [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(i)]]. You amended it with Center, so the ETA is 1400Z + 2:20 = 1620Z. The IAF is your clearance limit, so you hold there until about 1620Z.

questions.q: Your round-dial trainer has vacuum attitude and heading indicators and an electric turn coordinator. In IMC the alternator fails, and 40 minutes later the battery is dead and the radios go silent. Which flight instruments still work?
options: Attitude and heading indicators, plus airspeed, altimeter, VSI and compass
Only the turn coordinator and the magnetic compass
Turn coordinator, airspeed, altimeter and VSI, but no attitude or heading
Nothing but the magnetic compass, since every gyro needs electric power
questions.why: The vacuum pump is driven by the engine, so the vacuum attitude and heading indicators keep running [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Gyros are spread over separate electric and pneumatic sources, and many airplanes with air-driven attitude indicators use electric rate instruments [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. The turn coordinator's gyro is electric [[23:168|IFH 7-7]], so it is lost. Airspeed, altimeter and VSI run on pitot-static pressure [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. With the battery dead the transponder is off too, so just fly the 91.185 lost comm rules [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185]].

questions.q: Your heading indicator has failed. You are near 40° N latitude on a heading of 270° and turn right to north by compass, using 16° of bank. Using the IFH rule, at what compass reading do you start the rollout?
questions.why: Turning to north, the rollout lead is the latitude plus your normal lead of about half the bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. That is 40° + 8° = 48°, so start the rollout at 360° - 48° = 312°. Using the latitude alone gives 320°, and subtracting the lead (the rule for south) gives 328°.

questions.q: Your clearance limit is FIXX, an en route intersection, with an EFC of 1530Z. Your ETA from the filed ETE is 1500Z. The radios fail in IMC and you reach FIXX at 1445Z. FIXX to the IAF takes 10 minutes. What do you do?
options: Leave FIXX at 1450Z so you begin the approach right at your 1500Z ETA
Hold at FIXX until 1530Z, then fly to the IAF and begin the approach on arrival, about 1540Z
Leave FIXX on arrival at 1445Z, then hold at the IAF until 1530Z
Leave FIXX at 1520Z so you begin the approach at the IAF at 1530Z
questions.why: When the limit is not an approach fix and you have an EFC, leave the limit at the EFC. Then go to a fix where an approach begins and begin as close as possible to the ETA [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(ii)]]. You can't leave before 1530Z, and the 1500Z ETA has passed, so the closest you can come is to begin as soon as you reach the IAF, about 1540Z.

questions.q: In the glass-panel airplane the IFH uses as its example (its autopilot has a hidden turn coordinator), both the AHRS and the ADC fail in IMC. The PFD shows no flight data. What does the manufacturer recommend for the autopilot?
options: Turn it off, because every autopilot mode uses the failed AHRS
Engage altitude hold, which takes its data from the standby altimeter
Turn on the autopilot roll mode, a wing leveler fed by that turn coordinator
Couple it to the GPS course so it can fly the approach for you
questions.why: With an AHRS and ADC failure the manufacturer recommends turning on the autopilot, which is simply a wing leveler. Its roll mode uses a turn coordinator installed behind the MFD for the autopilot only. It cuts workload and the chance of an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

questions.q: Under 91.185 you broke out into VFR conditions and are heading for your towered destination. Your transmitter works, but you believe your receiver is dead. How do you arrive?
options: Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the traffic flow, then call the tower and ask for light signals
Fly straight in to the active runway, since the tower sees your 7600 code and will move traffic out of your way
Enter the Class D surface area and circle over the field without calling until you see a green light
Land at a nontowered airport instead, since a towered airport may not accept an airplane without a receiver
questions.why: With a dead receiver, remain outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the direction and flow of traffic. Then tell the tower your type, position, altitude and intention to land, and ask to be controlled with light signals. At 3 to 5 miles, report your position, join the pattern and watch the tower for lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

questions.q: After a vacuum failure you fly a VOR approach partial panel. The FAF altitude is 2,500 ft MSL, the TDZE is 400 ft, and the FAF to the MAP is 4.5 NM. Your groundspeed is 90 knots. What descent rate do you plan from the FAF?
options: About 470 fpm
About 830 fpm
About 600 fpm
About 700 fpm
questions.why: Subtract the TDZE from the FAF altitude and divide by the time inbound [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Time: 4.5 NM at 90 knots (1.5 NM per minute) = 3 minutes. Height: 2,500 - 400 = 2,100 ft. 2,100 ÷ 3 = 700 fpm. Dividing by the distance instead of the time gives about 470.

questions.q: Center cleared you to DUNES intersection via V3 and said, "expect further clearance via V12 to your destination." Beyond DUNES you had filed V9. The radios fail in IMC before DUNES. After DUNES, which route do you fly?
options: V9, the route in your flight plan
V12, the route ATC told you to expect
Direct to the destination by GPS, the shortest way
Whichever of V9 and V12 has the lower MEA
questions.why: With no assigned route beyond DUNES, the rule says to fly the route ATC advised may be expected in a further clearance. The filed route comes last, only when there is no assigned or expected route [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]].

questions.q: Flying partial panel after a vacuum failure, you look down to dig out a chart. When you look up, the airspeed is rising past 140 knots, the altimeter is unwinding and the turn coordinator shows a steep right turn. What is the correct recovery?
options: Pull back to raise the nose first, then level the wings and reduce power
Level the wings on the attitude indicator, then reduce power and raise the nose
Reduce power, level the wings on the turn coordinator, then raise the nose smoothly
Add power, lower the nose, then level the wings on the turn coordinator
questions.why: This is nose low. Reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure. The instinct is to pull back first [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The attitude indicator has failed, so recover with the airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Adding power and lowering the nose is the nose-high recovery.

questions.q: You are IFR in controlled airspace on a GPS route when your only VOR receiver fails. You don't need it for this flight. What must you do?
options: Nothing. Only failures of equipment you are using right now must be reported
Nothing in flight. Send a written report if the FAA asks for one
Report it only if the radios also fail, as part of a lost comm call
Report it to ATC as soon as practical, with the equipment and any help you want
questions.why: Report any in-flight malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical, including the aircraft identification, the equipment affected, how much your IFR ability is impaired, and the help you want [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. The AIM lists any loss of VOR receiver capability in controlled airspace [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

questions.q: You lost your heading indicator and are on a no-gyro surveillance approach. You are on final and the controller has told you to use half standard rate turns. You hear "turn left," then "stop turn" 8 seconds later. About how much did your heading change?
options: About 12°
About 24°
About 8°
About 4°
questions.why: After you are turned onto final on a surveillance or precision approach, ATC tells you to make half standard rate turns [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]]. Half standard rate is 1.5° per second (45° in 30 seconds) [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], so 8 seconds × 1.5° = 12°. A standard rate turn would give 24°.

questions.q: You are assigned 6,000 ft eastbound when the radios fail in IMC. At BRAVO the MEA rises to 9,000 ft, and BRAVO has an eastbound MCA of 8,000 ft. No other altitude was assigned or expected. What must you do?
options: Stay at 6,000 until BRAVO, then start the climb to 9,000
Climb early so you cross BRAVO at or above 8,000, then continue to 9,000
Climb to 8,000, the MCA, and keep it for the rest of the flight
Stay at 6,000, since you may not change altitude without a clearance
questions.why: Fly the highest of assigned, expected and minimum IFR altitude for each segment [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]], so 9,000 after BRAVO. Climb to a higher minimum IFR altitude right after passing the point where it applies, except that a fix with an MCA must be crossed at or above the MCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]]. The AIM example says the same: climb at the fix, or before it to meet an MCA [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]].

questions.q: In IMC your PFD screen goes blank and the MFD switches to reversionary mode. What do you lose, and what should you have been doing all along?
options: Engine data. You should have written down your normal power settings
Attitude and heading. You should have been flying the standby gauges
The moving map. You should have been following the flight on the en route chart
Nothing. The MFD now shows everything both screens showed before
questions.why: Reversionary mode puts the flight instruments and engine data on one screen and drops the moving map. The EFD does not replace en route charts, so follow the flight on the chart and know where the nearest airport is [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

questions.q: Your attitude and heading indicators fail in IMC. You are talking to Approach on squawk 4521 and decide to declare an emergency. What do you do with the transponder?
options: Change to 7700 right away so every facility sees the emergency
Keep 4521 unless ATC tells you to change it
Change to 7600, since your workload may stop you from talking
Set it to standby to save electrical power for the radios
questions.why: When you are in radio contact with an air traffic facility, keep squawking your assigned code and Mode C unless told otherwise. Squawk 7700 only if you can't reach a facility right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. 7600 is for a radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

questions.q: You are assigned 7,000 ft when the radios fail in IMC. Your cleared route first crosses a segment with an MEA of 9,000 ft, then joins an airway with an MEA of 5,000 ft. No other altitude was expected. What do you fly?
options: 7,000 the whole way, since it is your last assigned altitude
9,000 from the higher segment on, for the rest of the flight
9,000 on the higher segment, then 5,000, the MEA, on the airway
9,000 on the higher segment, then back down to 7,000 on the airway
questions.why: Fly the highest of assigned, expected and minimum IFR altitude for each segment [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]. The AIM example: climb to 9,000 where it becomes necessary, then on the 5,000 ft MEA airway descend to 7,000, the last assigned altitude, because it is higher than the MEA [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]].

questions.q: Before practicing timed turns, you calibrate the turn coordinator with a full panel. Holding what it shows as standard rate, your heading changes 24° every 10 seconds. What does this tell you?
options: You are turning slower than standard rate, so use a little more deflection
You are turning faster than standard rate, so use a little less deflection
It is close enough, since standard rate allows 20° to 30° per 10 seconds
The heading indicator has precessed, so reset it and ignore the result
questions.why: Standard rate is 30° in 10 seconds. If the airplane turns more or less than 30° in that time, use a larger or smaller deflection of the miniature aircraft to get standard rate, and use that corrected deflection in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. 24° is less, so you need a bit more.

questions.q: Your glass airplane's alternator fails in IMC. The standby battery switch is in ARM. Why might you turn off the MASTER side of the battery master/alternator switch?
options: To reset the alternator, since cycling the switch always restores charging
To charge the standby battery from the main battery before landing
To cut power to the transponder, which uses more power than the radios
To run the essential bus on the standby battery and save the main battery for landing
questions.why: Switching the MASTER side off takes the main battery offline, and the standby battery (if armed) powers the essential bus. That saves the main battery for the approach, so flaps and lights may still work. Don't count on any power after the standby battery is gone, and land as soon as practical [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

questions.q: You took off at 1320Z with a filed ETE of 1:45. Your clearance limit is the destination IAF and Center gave you an EFC of 1450Z. The radios fail in IMC and you reach the IAF at 1435Z. When should you begin descent and the approach?
options: On arrival at the IAF, at 1435Z
As close as possible to 1505Z, your ETA
As close as possible to 1450Z, your EFC
After one full lap in the hold, whatever the time is then
questions.why: When the clearance limit is a fix where an approach begins, begin descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the EFC if you received one. The ETA (here 1320Z + 1:45 = 1505Z) is used only when there is no EFC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(i)]]. Hold at the IAF until about 1450Z.

questions.q: After a vacuum failure you ask for a no-gyro surveillance (ASR) approach. What will the controller give you?
options: Headings plus glidepath calls, such as "slightly above glidepath"
Headings, when to descend to the MDA, the MAP and your distance each mile
Only the final approach course; you fly the descent from your chart
Headings to the FAF, then you finish the approach on the VOR
questions.why: An ASR gives guidance in azimuth only. The controller tells you when to descend to the MDA, where the MAP is, and your position each mile on final. Recommended altitudes each mile are given if you ask [[33:430|AIM 5-4-11]] [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]]. Glidepath calls come only on a PAR [[33:430|AIM 5-4-11]].

questions.q: In your glass airplane, the AFM says only Nav 1 and Com 1 run on standby battery power. You are planning a VOR approach in IMC. What setup does the IPH recommend?
options: Tune the approach VOR in Nav 1, the radio that keeps power on the battery
Tune the approach VOR in Nav 2, so Nav 1 stays free for the missed approach
Leave the VOR untuned until the FAF to save battery power
Tune the VOR in Nav 2 and switch it to Nav 1 only if the alternator fails
questions.why: Set up the instruments for the best chance of success after a vacuum or electrical failure. If only Nav 1 displays on battery or emergency power, put the primary NAVAID for the final approach in Nav 1 [[29:175|IPH 4-35]]. On many glass airplanes the essential bus on the standby battery powers Nav 1 and Com 1 [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

questions.q: You are partial panel in IMC, on vectors after a vacuum failure. Approach turns you toward final before you have briefed the approach, and you feel rushed. What is the best action?
options: Accept the turn and brief the approach after the FAF, once you are stable
Brief from memory so you don't add to the controller's workload
Engage the autopilot heading mode and brief while it flies
Ask Approach for a delay or extra vectors so you have time to brief
questions.why: A pilot who feels rushed while being vectored for an approach can ask for a delay or a vector that gives more time [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Briefing after the FAF or from memory adds risk, and a failing vacuum gyro connected to the autopilot can make it move the wrong way [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

questions.q: After a radio failure you reach ATC through an FSS relay, declare an emergency and get priority to land. You did not deviate from any rule. What report could you owe?
options: A written report to the FAA within 10 days, in every case
None, since no rule was broken
A detailed report within 48 hours to the ATC facility manager, if ATC asks
An NTSB report within 48 hours, because you declared an emergency
questions.why: A PIC who is given priority by ATC in an emergency, without deviating from a rule, must submit a detailed report within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]. A written report to the FAA applies when you deviate from a rule under 91.3(b), and only on request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]].
